title: Review: Gas exchange surfaces and SA:V in organisms; Gas exchange in fish, insects and plants; Water uptake and xerophytes; Human gas exchange and ventilation; Statistical tests
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX03b#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX01b#t2 term and clue written for the game; EX01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; EX12#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX01b#N.3, EX02a#N.11, EX03a#N.11, EX03b#N.4, PR03a#N.3, EX01b#N.5, EX02a#N.6, EX03a#N.3, PR03a#N.11, EX01b#N.11. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Spiracles
items.clue: Pores along an insect's thorax and abdomen that can close with valves

items.label: Ventilation
items.clue: Replacing the used air or water outside an exchange surface with fresh

items.label: Concentration gradient
items.clue: Kept steep by supply on one side of a surface and removal on the other

items.label: Spines
items.clue: What cactus leaves are reduced to, giving less surface for water loss.

questions.stem: A model exchange surface is changed. Its surface area is doubled and its thickness is tripled. The difference in concentration does not change. By what factor does the rate of diffusion change?
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ area ÷ thickness here, so the factor is 2 ÷ 3 = 0.67. The extra thickness outweighs the extra area.

questions.stem: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?

options.text: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.
The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
The diaphragm relaxes and rises into a dome, and the ribs move up so that air is drawn in to fill the space.

questions.explanation: Larger thorax volume, pressure in the lungs below atmospheric, and air flows in down the pressure gradient.

questions.stem: A water lily's leaves float flat on the surface of a pond. Where would you expect most of its stomata to be?

options.text: On the lower surface, touching the water, so the leaf can take in the water it needs through them.
Nowhere: the veins bring all the CO₂ the leaf needs up from the roots and the stem.
Nowhere: a thin, wet cuticle lets gases diffuse in across the whole leaf surface.
On the upper surface, because only that surface is in contact with the air.

questions.explanation: CO₂ diffuses far faster in air than in water. Stomata on the upper surface open straight onto the air.

questions.stem: In a model of one gill lamella, water enters with a relative O₂ concentration of 100 and blood enters with 0. Water and blood flow at equal rates and carry O₂ equally well. What is the highest value the blood could reach with each type of flow?

options.text: 100 with parallel flow; 100 with counter-current flow
50 with parallel flow; 50 with counter-current flow
50 with parallel flow; close to 100 with counter-current flow
Close to 100 with parallel flow; 50 with counter-current flow

questions.explanation: Parallel flow stops at equilibrium, 50. Counter-current flow keeps a gradient all along, so blood approaches the 100 of incoming water.

questions.stem: A student measures the lengths of 20 leaves from plants growing in the sun and 20 from plants growing in the shade. She wants to know whether mean leaf length differs between the two. Which statistical test should she use?

options.text: Chi-squared, because she is comparing two groups of plants.
Student's t-test, because she is comparing the means of two sets of continuous data.
A correlation coefficient, because she wants to know whether light is related to leaf length.
No test is needed: if the two means differ, the difference is real.

questions.explanation: Two groups, one measured variable, a difference in means: that is what the t-test is for.

questions.stem: Suppose that blood flow through the gill capillaries of an anaesthetised fish is stopped while water continues to flow over the gills, and that oxygen uptake across the gills falls almost to zero within a minute. Which explanation is best supported?

options.text: With no blood flow, oxygen built up in the stationary blood until its concentration matched the water's, so the gradient was lost.
Stopping blood flow cannot affect the gradient across the gill; the water flowing over the gills must have run out of oxygen.
Blood held still in the capillaries should load more fully, so the fall must have been caused by damage to the gill surface.
Oxygen enters with water absorbed into the blood, and once the blood stopped moving no more water could be taken up.

questions.stem: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?

options.text: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.
It houses the muscle that contracts to pump air in and out of the alveoli found at the end of every branch.

questions.stem: Which adaptation of a leaf allows carbon dioxide to reach the photosynthesising cells inside it?

options.text: The cuticle and epidermis are permeable to gases, so carbon dioxide diffuses in across the whole surface of the leaf.
The veins carry carbon dioxide into the leaf from the stem and roots and take the oxygen produced away.
Air spaces between the spongy mesophyll cells connect to the stomata, so the gas diffuses to every cell.
The palisade mesophyll lies just beneath the upper epidermis, so its cells absorb the gas from the outside air.

questions.explanation: CO₂ enters through the stomata, diffuses through the air spaces and dissolves in the moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells.

questions.stem: A 1999 study found that children who had slept with a light on before the age of two were more likely to become short-sighted later. Later studies found that short-sighted parents were more likely to leave a light on at night, and short sight is partly inherited. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Night-time lighting causes short sight, because the 1999 correlation was found in a large group of children.
The correlation can be explained by parents' short sight, which is linked to both variables.
The 1999 correlation must have been a mistake: the children with night lights were not really more short-sighted.
The later studies prove that light at night has no effect on the eye at all.

questions.stem: Lungless salamanders have no lungs and, as adults, no gills. They exchange gases across their skin and the lining of the mouth. Which set of features would best suit this way of life?

options.text: Dry, thick skin, so that gases cross it as gases without having to dissolve first.
Thin, moist skin over a dense capillary network, with blood flowing through it continuously.
A large, bulky body, so that the total area of skin available for gas exchange is as large as possible.
Slow blood flow through the skin, so that each red blood cell has time to fill with oxygen.
